steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on explaining embedding-based entity alignment between knowledge graphs and using the explanations to repair alignment results. It should cover background, the challenges, our framework ExEA, contributions, and a section outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Entity alignment (EA) background and embedding-based EA
- Recent embedding-based EA work; lack of explainability
- Challenges
- Solution: ExEA
- Contributions
- Outline

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - EA: find identical entities across KGs; multi-source knowledge sharing/transfer for downstream apps
  - long-standing in database and Semantic Web fields
  - early: string matching + similarity propagation
  - deep learning -> entity embeddings, nearest neighbor search in vector space
  - encoders: TransE, GCNs; similarity from output vectors
  - inference: source entity e_{1}, greedily pick most similar e_{2} in target KG
- Recent work + motivation
  - increasing attention; hundreds of studies
  - representation learning: relational GCNs, multi-hop GCNs, dual GCNs
  - inference: bi-directional k NN search, reinforcement learning, holistic matching
  - embedding-based EA unexplainable, like other deep models; no prior effort on EA explanations
  - explanations: insight into differences between models; background knowledge to judge reliability
- Challenges
  - (1) no prior research; existing explanation methods find most influential input features; EA output (e_{1}\equiv e_{2}) depends on features (relation triples) of both entities -> not directly applicable
  - (2) model complexity: GCN-based models use high-order triples; enumerating multi-order combinations is time-consuming
  - (3) using explanations to repair results; first attempt to use explanation feedback
- Solution: ExEA
  - explanations as semantic matching subgraphs (heuristic cognition of EA), consistent triples around both entities
  - all matching triples treated as important features -> skip evaluating combined feature influence
  - saves time; unbiased, faithful to model
  - alignment dependency graph (ADG) -> explanation confidence -> resolve conflicts, repair
- Contributions
  - definition of explanation for embedding-based EA (fidelity)
  - ExEA: extensible, high-quality explanations, repairs results, any embedding-based model
  - four representative EA models, benchmark datasets
  - findings: simple models + repair = high accuracy; one-to-many most common/influential conflict; some alignment not identifiable from structure in the benchmark
- Outline: II notations/definitions/pipeline; III explanation generation; IV repair; V experiments; VI related work; VII conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Entity alignment (EA) is the task of finding identical entities in different knowledge graphs (KGs). It can help multi-source knowledge sharing and transfer, which better supports downstream applications. EA is a long-standing task in the database and Semantic Web fields. Early work on EA mostly used string matching to compute entity similarity and then inferred EA via similarity propagation. With the development of deep learning techniques, recent work represents entities as vectors (i.e., embeddings) and finds EA with nearest neighbor search in the vector space. Usually embedding-based EA models use shallow or deep neural networks, e.g., TransE or graph convolutional networks (GCNs), to encode entities, and they use the output vectors to compute the similarity between entities. In the alignment inference phase, given a source entity e_{1} to be aligned, the model usually greedily picks the most similar entity e_{2} in the target KG as the counterpart.

Embedding-based EA has recently got more and more attention. Hundreds of studies in the last several years have explored advanced representation learning techniques, like relational GCNs, multi-hop GCNs, and dual GCNs, to train informative entity embeddings for computing similarity. Other studies improved EA inference with bi-directional k NN search, reinforcement learning, and holistic matching. But embedding-based EA models are unexplainable, like other deep learning models, and we can't see the reasoning behind their output. Still, there has been no effort to provide explanations for EA. Understanding embedding-based EA results can give deep insight into the differences between EA models. EA explanations can also serve as background knowledge that helps users judge whether EA results are reliable. So in this paper we study EA explanations.

Challenges. Explaining embedding-based EA results is hard. The first challenge is that there is no prior research. Existing explanation approaches for machine learning algorithms try to find the most influential input features that can change the result. For EA, an alignment output (e.g., e_{1}\equiv e_{2}) is determined by the features (i.e., relation triples) of both entities. So existing explanation approaches can't be applied directly to embedding-based EA. The second challenge is that embedding-based EA models are complex. GCN-based EA models usually use high-order triples for alignment inference. Enumerating all possible combinations of multi-order triples takes a lot of time, so it is difficult to measure how important each triple is for the EA result. The third challenge is how to use explanations to repair the model results. As far as we know, this is the first attempt that takes explanation feedback into account, which makes it possible to use explanation generation methods in real-world situations.

Challenges.
- no prior research; existing explanation methods find influential input features; EA depends on triples of both entities
- GCN-based models use high-order triples; enumeration time-consuming
- repairing results with explanations; first attempt with explanation feedback

Solution: ExEA
- semantic matching subgraphs; all matching triples as important features
- saves time, unbiased, faithful
- ADG -> explanation confidence -> resolve conflicts, repair

Contributions: definition; ExEA (extensible, repair, any model); four models on benchmarks; three findings

Outline: Sections II-VII

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Entity alignment (EA) is the task of finding identical entities in different knowledge graphs (KGs). It can help multi-source knowledge sharing and transfer, which better supports downstream applications. EA is a long-standing task in the database and Semantic Web fields. Early work on EA mostly used string matching to compute entity similarity and then inferred EA via similarity propagation. With the development of deep learning techniques, recent work represents entities as vectors (i.e., embeddings) and finds EA with nearest neighbor search in the vector space. Usually embedding-based EA models use shallow or deep neural networks, e.g., TransE or graph convolutional networks (GCNs), to encode entities, and they use the output vectors to compute the similarity between entities. In the alignment inference phase, given a source entity e_{1} to be aligned, the model usually greedily picks the most similar entity e_{2} in the target KG as the counterpart.

Embedding-based EA has recently got more and more attention. Hundreds of studies in the last several years have explored advanced representation learning techniques, like relational GCNs, multi-hop GCNs, and dual GCNs, to train informative entity embeddings for computing similarity. Other studies improved EA inference with bi-directional k NN search, reinforcement learning, and holistic matching. But embedding-based EA models are unexplainable, like other deep learning models, and we can't see the reasoning behind their output. Still, there has been no effort to provide explanations for EA. Understanding embedding-based EA results can give deep insight into the differences between EA models. EA explanations can also serve as background knowledge that helps users judge whether EA results are reliable. So in this paper we study EA explanations.

Challenges. Explaining embedding-based EA results is hard. The first challenge is that there is no prior research. Existing explanation approaches for machine learning algorithms try to find the most influential input features that can change the result. For EA, an alignment output (e.g., e_{1}\equiv e_{2}) is determined by the features (i.e., relation triples) of both entities. So existing explanation approaches can't be applied directly to embedding-based EA. The second challenge is that embedding-based EA models are complex. GCN-based EA models usually use high-order triples for alignment inference. Enumerating all possible combinations of multi-order triples takes a lot of time, so it is difficult to measure how important each triple is for the EA result. The third challenge is how to use explanations to repair the model results. As far as we know, this is the first attempt that takes explanation feedback into account, which makes it possible to use explanation generation methods in real-world situations.

Solution. To deal with these challenges, we present the ExEA framework in this paper. Based on the heuristic cognition of the EA task, ExEA treats generating EA explanations as generating semantic matching subgraphs, which can consider the characteristics of both entities at the same time by matching semantically consistent triples around them. To give comprehensive explanations, ExEA treats all the matching triples as important features. This lets us skip evaluating how combined features influence the model. This saves a lot of time, and it also keeps the generated explanations unbiased and faithful to the original model, without biases that could come from estimating feature importance. After we get the explanation, we design an alignment dependency graph structure (ADG) to understand the explanation more deeply. With this graph we can calculate the explanation confidence, which is very important for resolving conflicts in EA results and repairing them.

Contributions. Our main contributions are:

- We give a definition of the explanation for embedding-based EA, which considers the fidelity of EA results.

- We propose ExEA, an extensible framework that can generate high quality explanations for a given EA model. It can also repair the EA results. ExEA can be applied to any embedding-based EA model.

- We put four representative EA models into ExEA and evaluate their effectiveness on benchmark datasets.

- We have several findings on embedding-based EA. First, simple models can also get high accuracy if alignment conflicts are repaired effectively. Second, the one-to-many alignment is the most common and the most influential conflict. Third, some alignment in the benchmark cannot be identified based on structures.

Outline. Section II introduces notations, definitions, and the pipeline of ExEA. Section III describes our explanation generation method and Section IV describes our EA repair method. Section V has the experiments and Section VI discusses related work. Section VII concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Entity alignment (EA) is the task of finding identical entities in different knowledge graphs (KGs). It can promote multi-source knowledge sharing and transfer to better support downstream applications. EA is a long-standing task in the database and Semantic Web fields. Early work on EA mainly used string matching to compute entity similarity and inferred EA via similarity propagation [1,2]. The development of deep learning techniques has motivated recent work to represent entities as vectors (i.e., embeddings) and find EA using nearest neighbor search in vector space [3]. Typically, embedding-based EA models use shallow or deep neural networks, e.g., TransE [4] or graph convolutional networks (GCNs) [5], to encode entities, and use the output vector representations to compute the similarity between entities. In the alignment inference phase, given a source entity e_{1} to be aligned, the model usually greedily selects the most similar entity e_{2} in the target KG as its counterpart.

Recently, embedding-based EA has attracted increasing attention [6,7]. Hundreds of studies in the past several years have explored advanced representation learning techniques, such as relational GCNs [8], multi-hop GCNs [9], and dual GCNs [10], to train informative entity embeddings for similarity computation, while others have improved EA inference via bi-directional k NN search [11], reinforcement learning [12,13], and holistic matching [14,15]. However, like other deep learning models, embedding-based EA models are unexplainable: we cannot discern the reasoning behind their output. Yet no effort has been made to provide explanations for EA. Understanding embedding-based EA results can offer insight into the distinctions between EA models, and EA explanations can act as background knowledge that helps users judge the reliability of EA results. We therefore study EA explanations in this paper.

Challenges. Explaining embedding-based EA results is challenging. The first challenge is the absence of prior research. Existing explanation approaches for machine learning algorithms strive to discover the most influential input features that can change the result [16]. In EA, however, an alignment output (e.g., e_{1}\equiv e_{2}) is determined by the features (i.e., relation triples) of both entities, so existing explanation approaches cannot be directly applied to embedding-based EA. The second challenge lies in the complexity of embedding-based EA models. GCN-based EA models [10] usually consider high-order triples for alignment inference, and it is time-consuming to enumerate all possible combinations of multi-order triples, making it difficult to measure the importance of each triple to the EA result. The third challenge is how to use explanations to repair model results. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to take explanation feedback into account, making it possible to use explanation generation methods in real-world situations.

Solution. To resolve these challenges, we present the ExEA framework. Based on the heuristic cognition of the EA task, ExEA regards the generation of EA explanations as the generation of semantic matching subgraphs, which take into account the characteristics of both entities simultaneously by matching semantically consistent triples around them. To provide comprehensive explanations, ExEA treats all matching triples as important features, which lets us bypass evaluating the influence of combined features on the model. This not only saves considerable time but also keeps the generated explanations unbiased and faithful to the original model, unaffected by biases that might arise when estimating feature importance. After obtaining the explanation, we devise an alignment dependency graph structure (ADG) to gain deeper insight into it. Using this graph, we can calculate the explanation confidence, which plays a crucial role in resolving conflicts in EA results and repairing them effectively.

Contributions. Our main contributions are as follows:

- We provide a definition of the explanation for embedding-based EA that considers the fidelity of EA results.

- We propose ExEA, an extensible framework that generates high quality explanations for a given EA model and can also repair its EA results. ExEA can be applied to any embedding-based EA model.

- We incorporate four representative EA models into ExEA and evaluate their effectiveness on benchmark datasets.

- We make several findings on embedding-based EA. First, simple models can also achieve high accuracy by effectively repairing alignment conflicts. Second, one-to-many alignment is the most common and most influential conflict. Third, some alignment in the benchmark [17] cannot be identified based on structures.

Outline. Section II introduces notations, definitions, and the pipeline of ExEA. We describe our explanation generation method in Section III and our EA repair method in Section IV. Section V presents experiments and Section VI discusses related work. Finally, Section VII concludes the paper.
